Mixture-of-Memories: Low-Overhead Language Modeling with Modular Knowledge Injection

Yifan Lu Affiliation: MBZUAI, Abu Dhabi, UAE    Rubin Wei Affiliation: LUMIA Lab, School of Artificial Intelligence, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, China    Ziyun Zou Affiliation: MBZUAI, Abu Dhabi, UAE    Junhong Liang Affiliation: MBZUAI, Abu Dhabi, UAE    Haolin Yang Affiliation: MBZUAI, Abu Dhabi, UAE    Xinlin Zhuang Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong    Abhijit Das Affiliation: MBZUAI, Abu Dhabi, UAE    Adinath Madhavrao Dukre Affiliation: MBZUAI, Abu Dhabi, UAE    Shadab Khan Affiliation: ADIA Lab, Abu Dhabi, UAE    Zhouhan Lin Affiliation: LUMIA Lab, School of Artificial Intelligence, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, China    Imran Razzak Corresponding author: Imran Razzak; Email: Imran.Razzak@mbzuai.ac.ae Affiliation: MBZUAI, Abu Dhabi, UAE
Abstract

Large language models store substantial factual knowledge in their parameters, yet this knowledge is difficult to control, update, and reliably elicit at inference time. Existing memory-augmented approaches typically rely on a single auxiliary mechanism, such as retrieval, parameter updates, or neural memory, and therefore apply the same form of correction to tokens with very different knowledge demands. We propose Mixture-of-Memories (MoM), a memory-augmented language modeling framework that separates routed neural memory from writable factual memory. MoM combines a frozen base LM with two neural memory experts: a latent memory that provides low-latency hidden-state corrections and a lexical memory that provides a token-space knowledge pathway. A lightweight Budget Router sets per-token mixture weights from uncertainty and disagreement features, replacing the fixed interpolation of prior memory modules. For post-hoc updates, an external explicit memory stays outside the router, because a router trained before facts are written learns to down-weight it; new facts are appended without retraining any component and used only when an answer-level gate accepts the retrieved fact. Experiments across language modeling, factual QA, update analysis, and efficiency show that MoM improves both predictive accuracy and updateability while retaining low inference overhead.

Keywords: Parametric Memory, Knowledge Updating, Token-Level Routing

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) encode a substantial amount of world knowledge in their parameters (Allen-Zhu and Li, 2025). This capability follows from large-scale next-token prediction and is one reason pretrained LMs generalize well. Parametric knowledge, however, is a poor interface for knowledge-intensive prediction. Parameters are optimized to capture broad statistical regularities, not to give explicit control over how individual facts are stored, accessed, or updated. The mechanism that handles common linguistic and factual patterns therefore becomes unreliable when a prediction depends on precise, infrequent, or newly introduced knowledge (Chang et al., 2024, Gekhman et al., 2024, Ovadia et al., 2024), which leaves a gap between what an LLM absorbs during pretraining and what it can reliably use at inference time.

This gap has at least three sources. A fact may be weakly represented because it is under-supported in pretraining, difficult to recover because the context does not elicit it, or stale because it changed after training. Existing approaches address these failure modes only partially. Parameter-side methods internalize new information into model weights, but frequent or repeated updates remain difficult to support cleanly (Wang et al., 2024c). External retrieval and token-level memory make updates easier but add search and context-processing overhead at inference time (Cao et al., 2026). Latent-space memory compresses information into hidden representations and can improve retention, but it is tied to model-specific representations (Wang et al., 2024b, Wang et al., 2025). Plug-and-play parametric memories imitate non-parametric retrievers with lightweight auxiliary modules, which improves portability and inference efficiency, yet they still expose a single auxiliary path with fixed interpolation (Cao et al., 2026, Wei et al., 2025).

Because all of these mechanisms ultimately act through next-token prediction at inference time, their differences matter only insofar as they change the local prediction problem during generation. The need for extra knowledge is not uniform across positions. At many steps, the base LM is already sufficient: the next token is governed mainly by local syntax, common lexical patterns, or highly reinforced knowledge, so auxiliary support brings little benefit. The challenging cases are concentrated on a much smaller subset of positions where prediction depends on precise factual content, such as entities, numbers, dates, and other knowledge-bearing slots (Yao et al., 2025). Even there, the relevant deficiency is not always the same. Some errors reflect weak parametric support and call for a lightweight correction to the base prediction; others reflect a need for more explicit token-level guidance or direct access to facts introduced after pretraining. This makes a single global augmentation rule difficult to justify. If the same auxiliary correction is applied uniformly throughout generation, the model is forced to treat easy and difficult positions alike, and to use the same form of support for qualitatively different failure modes. A more natural formulation is to let knowledge support vary with the local prediction state, invoking different auxiliary paths only where they are likely to reduce token-level error.

To bridge the gap, we propose Mixture-of-Memories (MoM), a memory-augmented language modeling framework that separates memory for stable prediction from memory for post-hoc updates. MoM combines a frozen base LM with two routed neural memory experts: a latent memory (LatM) that provides low-latency, retrieval-like corrections in hidden space, and a lexical memory (LexM) that operates in token space and is therefore less coupled to the backbone’s representations. A lightweight Budget Router assigns token-wise mixture weights over these stable sources from uncertainty and disagreement features. Mutable knowledge goes to an explicit memory (ExpM), an external store that is kept outside the router; it retrieves a stored fact once per question and injects its answer only when an answer-level gate judges the fact reliable. Facts are added by appending entries, without retraining the backbone, the neural memories, or the router.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose Mixture-of-Memories, which composes a frozen base language model with a latent and a lexical memory through a lightweight token-wise Budget Router.

  • •

    We keep mutable knowledge in an explicit memory outside the router, so new facts can be written without retraining the backbone, the neural memories, or the router, and take effect immediately.

  • •

    Extensive experiments show that MoM reduces WikiText-103 perplexity on GPT2-large from 10.45 to 9.37, improves the average factual QA score over frozen backbones by 15.6% on Mistral-7B and 10.9% on Llama-3.1-8B, and lowers time to first token by 2.9–3.0×\times relative to retrieval-augmented baselines on a 7B backbone.

2 Related Work

Retrieval-augmented generation.

Retrieval-augmented generation grounds predictions in external knowledge. RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) retrieves documents or passages, RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022) retrieves corpus chunks, and kkNN-LM (Khandelwal et al., 2020) retrieves nearest-neighbor continuations from a datastore of activations. Recent work post-trains the reader to make better use of retrieved evidence, through hierarchical-thought instruction tuning in HIRAG (Jiao et al., 2025) or reinforcement learning with a curriculum in RAG-RL (Huang et al., 2025). These methods keep knowledge explicit and easy to refresh, but they shift cost to inference: online search adds latency, retrieved evidence lengthens the context, and large indexes or datastores require storage. MoM amortizes retrieval-like corrections into neural memory experts that are invoked through token-wise routing, and it reserves explicit lookup for a small store of written facts.

Parametric long-term memory.

Parametric memory methods reduce the serving cost of retrieval by compressing corpus-level knowledge into learned auxiliary modules. MLP Memory (Wei et al., 2025) uses an external MLP to mimic non-parametric retrieval, and Memory Decoder (Cao et al., 2026) attaches a plug-and-play decoder memory to a frozen language model. Both make memory access fast and model-compatible, but compressing knowledge into parameters gives up direct writability, one of the main advantages of retrieval: adding or revising facts requires retraining, re-distillation, or rebuilding the memory. MoM keeps parametric memories for stable, low-latency modeling and delegates factual updates to a separate explicit memory.

Conditional computation and knowledge editing.

Sparse mixture-of-experts models route tokens to experts to scale capacity (Shazeer et al., 2017, Fedus et al., 2022, Du et al., 2022). MoM instead routes among heterogeneous knowledge sources, namely the base LM, a hidden-space memory, and a token-space memory, for conditional memory access. For editing, MEND (Mitchell et al., 2022a), ROME (Meng et al., 2022), and MEMIT (Meng et al., 2023) modify model weights, whereas SERAC (Mitchell et al., 2022b), GRACE (Hartvigsen et al., 2023), and WISE (Wang et al., 2024a) store edits in auxiliary modules. ExpM is closest to the second group, but it writes facts as raw key–value entries without per-edit optimization.

3 Methodology

MoM is built on a separation principle: stable neural memories are routed, while mutable explicit knowledge is injected externally. The two kinds of memory serve different purposes. Neural memories are trained once and reused across inputs, which makes them suitable for token-level routing. Explicit memory is sparse, user- or time-dependent, and may be empty during router training but populated at test time. Placing such a store in the same router softmax lets the router learn that explicit memory is useless whenever the store is empty (Section 4.3). MoM therefore consists of a routed neural memory core and an external explicit memory overlay (Figure 2).

Given a context x≤t=(x1,…,xt)x_{\leq t}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}), the model predicts the next token yt=xt+1y_{t}=x_{t+1}. The routed core consists of three stable sources,

𝒞={Base,LatM,LexM},\mathcal{C}=\{\mathrm{Base},\mathrm{LatM},\mathrm{LexM}\}, (1)

where Base\mathrm{Base} is the frozen parametric memory of the language model, LatM\mathrm{LatM} is a latent-space memory distilled from retrieval behavior, and LexM\mathrm{LexM} is a token-space lexical memory.

MoM first builds a core distribution by routing among the stable sources:

where pmp_{m} is the distribution produced by source mm and πm​(t)\pi_{m}(t) is a token-dependent routing weight. The conditioning of pmp_{m} is module-specific: Base and LexM consume the token sequence, while LatM consumes a hidden representation extracted from the frozen base model.

When the gate rejects, dt=0d_{t}=0 and Eq. 3 reduces exactly to the routed core. Neither dtd_{t} nor λt\lambda_{t} is produced by the Budget Router.

3.2 Routed Neural Memory Core

Base memory.

The base source is a frozen autoregressive language model with parameters θBase\theta_{\mathrm{Base}}. It produces logits zBase​(t)=FθBase​(x≤t)z_{\mathrm{Base}}(t)=F_{\theta_{\mathrm{Base}}}(x_{\leq t}) and the next-token distribution

pBase​(yt∣x≤t)=softmax​(zBase​(t))yt.p_{\mathrm{Base}}(y_{t}\mid x_{\leq t})=\mathrm{softmax}\big(z_{\mathrm{Base}}(t)\big)_{y_{t}}. (4)

The base model also provides a hidden representation

ht=ϕθBase(ℓ)​(x≤t)h_{t}=\phi_{\theta_{\mathrm{Base}}}^{(\ell)}(x_{\leq t}) (5)

from a fixed layer ℓ\ell. LatM and the ExpM encoders reuse hidden states from the same backbone forward pass, while LexM takes the token sequence as input.

Latent memory.

LatM removes the online nearest-neighbor search of retrieval-augmented LMs. Instead of searching a datastore at every token, it learns a parametric approximation of retrieval-style corrections in the hidden space of the base model:

pLatM​(yt∣ht)=softmax​(GLatM​(ht))yt.p_{\mathrm{LatM}}(y_{t}\mid h_{t})=\mathrm{softmax}\big(G_{\mathrm{LatM}}(h_{t})\big)_{y_{t}}. (6)

GLatMG_{\mathrm{LatM}} is a lightweight MLP-style memory module. It is trained by distilling retrieval-augmented teacher distributions and frozen afterwards, and it provides low-latency corrections when the base representation already contains enough signal to predict the needed retrieval behavior.

Lexical memory.

LexM complements LatM by operating in token space rather than in the hidden space of the base model:

pLexM​(yt∣x≤t)=softmax​(DecLexM​(x≤t))yt.p_{\mathrm{LexM}}(y_{t}\mid x_{\leq t})=\mathrm{softmax}\big(\mathrm{Dec}_{\mathrm{LexM}}(x_{\leq t})\big)_{y_{t}}. (7)

Because LexM consumes token IDs rather than hidden states, it does not depend on the representation geometry of a particular base model. LatM is efficient but base-specific, whereas LexM can be attached to another backbone with a compatible vocabulary (Appendix B.1). After training, LexM is frozen and becomes a stable source of the routed core.

3.3 Budget Router

The Budget Router decides when each stable source should influence the next-token distribution. It outputs a distribution over the routed core:

log⁡𝝅⁡(t)=LogSoftmax⁡(Rψ​(ft)),\log\boldsymbol{\pi}(t)=\mathrm{LogSoftmax}\big(R_{\psi}(f_{t})\big), (8)

where 𝝅⁡(t)=[πBase​(t),πLatM​(t),πLexM​(t)]\boldsymbol{\pi}(t)=[\pi_{\mathrm{Base}}(t),\pi_{\mathrm{LatM}}(t),\pi_{\mathrm{LexM}}(t)], RψR_{\psi} is an MLP, and ftf_{t} contains inexpensive uncertainty and disagreement features:

ft=[HBase​(t),marginBase​(t),JSD⁡(pBase,pLatM)​(t),JSD⁡(pBase,pLexM)​(t)].f_{t}=\big[\,H_{\mathrm{Base}}(t),\ \mathrm{margin}_{\mathrm{Base}}(t),\ \operatorname{JSD}(p_{\mathrm{Base}},p_{\mathrm{LatM}})(t),\ \operatorname{JSD}(p_{\mathrm{Base}},p_{\mathrm{LexM}})(t)\,\big]. (9)

The core mixture is computed in log space with the log-sum-exp operator, LSEm(am)=log∑mexp(am)\operatorname{LSE}_{m}(a_{m})=\log\sum_{m}\exp(a_{m}):

log⁡pcore​(yt∣x≤t)=LSEm∈𝒞⁡[log⁡πm​(t)+log⁡pm​(yt∣x≤t)].\log p_{\mathrm{core}}(y_{t}\mid x_{\leq t})=\operatorname{LSE}_{m\in\mathcal{C}}\big[\log\pi_{m}(t)+\log p_{m}(y_{t}\mid x_{\leq t})\big]. (10)

ExpM is deliberately absent from Eq. 8 because it is mutable and may be empty while the router is trained, so routing it would teach the router to suppress explicit memory.

3.4 External Explicit Memory

ExpM stores facts as writable entries. A fact consists of a question or prompt xix_{i} and its answer token sequence ai=(ai,1,…,ai,Mi)a_{i}=(a_{i,1},\ldots,a_{i,M_{i}}). Each entry keeps a dense key kik_{i}, a TF-IDF vector k~i\tilde{k}_{i} of xix_{i}, the answer aia_{i}, and a source record. Adding knowledge appends entries to the store Δ\Delta and changes no parameter of the base model, LatM, LexM, the router, or the ExpM encoders.

Query and key encoders.

ExpM reads the frozen backbone rather than raw text. At position tt it forms the feature

zt=[ht;h¯t],z_{t}=\big[\,h_{t}\,;\ \bar{h}_{t}\,\big], (11)

where hth_{t} is the backbone hidden state of Eq. 5 and h¯t\bar{h}_{t} is the mean hidden state of the most recent valid tokens. Two separate towers EqE_{q} and EkE_{k} map this feature to L2-normalized vectors. The query q=Eq​(zT)q=E_{q}(z_{T}) is taken at the last position TT of the question, where the answer starts, and the key of a fact, ki=Ek​(z⁡(xi))k_{i}=E_{k}(z(x_{i})), is taken at the last position of its own question prefix.

Retrieval.

ExpM retrieves once per question, before the answer is generated. Each entry is scored by a convex combination of dense and lexical similarity,

si=(1−β)q⊤​ki+12+βcos(q~,k~i),s_{i}=(1-\beta)\,\frac{q^{\top}k_{i}+1}{2}+\beta\,\cos\big(\tilde{q},\tilde{k}_{i}\big), (12)

where q~\tilde{q} is the TF-IDF vector of the question and β∈[0,1]\beta\in[0,1] weights the lexical term. Rescaling the dense cosine to [0,1][0,1] puts both terms on the same range. ExpM takes the highest-scoring entry i⋆i^{\star} over the whole store as its answer candidate. The top-kk entries 𝒩\mathcal{N} under the same score serve to compute gate features.

Answer-level gate.

Retrieval always returns a candidate, including for questions whose fact is not in the store, so ExpM must decide whether to trust it. A logistic-regression gate estimates the probability that the retrieved answer is correct:

g(x)=σ(𝐰⊤ϕ(x)+b),d=𝟏[g(x)≥η].g(x)=\sigma\big(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}(x)+b\big),\qquad d=\mathbf{1}\big[g(x)\geq\eta\big]. (13)

The features ϕ⁡(x)\boldsymbol{\phi}(x) are the retrieval score si⋆​(x)s_{i^{\star}}(x), its margin over the second-best candidate, the lexical overlap between xx and xi⋆x_{i^{\star}}, the agreement among the answers in 𝒩\mathcal{N}, and the probability that the routed core assigns to the first retrieved answer token, pcore​(ai⋆,1∣x)p_{\mathrm{core}}(a_{i^{\star},1}\mid x). The last feature lets the gate weigh the retrieval evidence against the core’s own prediction.

Answer injection.

The gate decision holds for the whole answer, with dt=dd_{t}=d at every answer position. If the gate accepts, ExpM proposes the stored answer token by token, followed by the end-of-sequence token. At the jj-th answer position,

pExpM(yt∣x≤t,Δ)=𝟏[yt=ai⋆,j],p_{\mathrm{ExpM}}(y_{t}\mid x_{\leq t},\Delta)=\mathbf{1}\big[y_{t}=a_{i^{\star},j}\big], (14)

and Eq. 3 is applied with λt=0.8\lambda_{t}=0.8. Because pExpMp_{\mathrm{ExpM}} is a point mass and λt>0.5\lambda_{t}>0.5, the proposed token always receives the highest probability, so greedy decoding reproduces the retrieved answer exactly; the overlay then acts as gated answer copying. If the gate rejects, dt=0d_{t}=0 throughout and the routed core generates the answer alone.

3.5 Training

MoM is trained in stages so that each component is optimized for its role.

Teacher construction.

We first construct a retrieval-augmented teacher distribution

p∗​(yt∣x≤t)=(1−λret)​pBase​(yt∣x≤t)+λret​pret​(yt∣x≤t),p^{*}(y_{t}\mid x_{\leq t})=(1-\lambda_{\mathrm{ret}})\,p_{\mathrm{Base}}(y_{t}\mid x_{\leq t})+\lambda_{\mathrm{ret}}\,p_{\mathrm{ret}}(y_{t}\mid x_{\leq t}), (15)

where pretp_{\mathrm{ret}} is an offline kkNN retrieval distribution. Interpolating with the base model reduces the brittleness of pure retrieval supervision while exposing the neural memories to retrieval-like corrections.

Neural memory distillation.

LatM and LexM are trained to match the teacher while preserving next-token accuracy. For each m∈{LatM,LexM}m\in\{\mathrm{LatM},\mathrm{LexM}\}, we minimize

ℒdistillm=μKL(p∗∥pm)+(1−μ)CE(pm,yt).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{distill}}^{m}=\mu\,\operatorname{KL}\big(p^{*}\,\|\,p_{m}\big)+(1-\mu)\,\operatorname{CE}\big(p_{m},y_{t}\big). (16)

After distillation, Base, LatM, and LexM are frozen.

Router training.

With all core distributions fixed, only the router parameters ψ\psi are trained:

ℒrouter=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{router}}={} 𝔼t​[−log⁡pcore​(yt∣x≤t)]+βLexM​𝔼t​[πLexM​(t)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[-\log p_{\mathrm{core}}(y_{t}\mid x_{\leq t})\big]+\beta_{\mathrm{LexM}}\,\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\pi_{\mathrm{LexM}}(t)\big] (17)
+γ​𝔼t​[‖𝝅⁡(t)−𝝅⁡(t−1)‖1]−λent​𝔼t​[H⁡(𝝅⁡(t))].\displaystyle+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\|\boldsymbol{\pi}(t)-\boldsymbol{\pi}(t-1)\|_{1}\big]-\lambda_{\mathrm{ent}}\,\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[H(\boldsymbol{\pi}(t))\big].

The likelihood term teaches the router which source improves prediction. The LexM budget term discourages unnecessary use of the heavier token-space decoder, the smoothness term stabilizes decisions across adjacent tokens, and the entropy term prevents collapse to a single source.

Explicit memory.

The ExpM encoders are trained once and then frozen. During this stage, λt\lambda_{t} in Eq. 3 is produced by a token-level gate, and the encoders and gate minimize

ℒExpM=ℒnce+ℒnll+ℒloc.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ExpM}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{nce}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{nll}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{loc}}. (18)

ℒnce\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{nce}} is an InfoNCE loss: the query at the answer start is compared with the unmasked candidate keys through q⊤​kj/τq^{\top}k_{j}/\tau with temperature τ\tau, and the cross-entropy target is the key of the question’s own fact. ℒnll\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{nll}} is the mean negative log-likelihood of the gold answer tokens under the mixed distribution of Eq. 3, computed on examples whose fact is in the store. ℒloc\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{loc}} averages −log⁡(1−λt)-\log(1-\lambda_{t}) over the answer positions of examples whose fact is absent from the store and of locality examples, so the gate learns to close when memory should not be used. Writing a fact (x,a)(x,a) requires no gradient update:

Δ←Δ∪{(Ek​(z⁡(x)),k~​(x),a)}.\Delta\leftarrow\Delta\cup\big\{\big(E_{k}(z(x)),\ \tilde{k}(x),\ a\big)\big\}. (19)

At inference time, MoM computes the three core distributions, routes them into pcorep_{\mathrm{core}}, and applies the ExpM overlay of Eq. 3 when the gate accepts the retrieved fact.

4 Experiments

We first report factual QA results, then attribute the gains to individual memory channels, analyze how ExpM absorbs updates, and finally measure efficiency. Appendix B.1 reports the transfer of LexM across backbones.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets.

For language modeling we use WikiText-103 (Merity et al., 2017). For factual QA we evaluate on the full evaluation splits of NQ (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019), WebQuestions (WebQ; Berant et al., 2013), TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022), and HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018). Wikipedia-2021 (Izacard et al., 2023) is the corpus for memory training, continued pretraining, the kkNN-LM datastore, and RAG retrieval. Appendix A.1 and Appendix A.3 give dataset and metric details.

Baselines.

We compare MoM with the frozen base LM and with two groups of methods. The parametric group comprises full continued pretraining (CPT), LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), and MLP Memory (Wei et al., 2025). The retrieval group comprises RAG with a BGE retriever (Xiao et al., 2024) that prepends the top-5 Wikipedia passages, kkNN-LM with a 50M-key datastore, and a paper-guided reproduction of RAG-RL (Huang et al., 2025). MLP Memory is reported for Mistral only. Its official release provides Mistral checkpoints but no Llama-3.1-8B checkpoint, and rebuilding its backbone-specific hidden-state datastore over billions of Wikipedia tokens exceeded our storage budget. Appendix A.2 specifies all configurations.

Implementation.

We use Mistral-7B-v0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023) and Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) as the main backbones and GPT2-large (Radford et al., 2019) for controlled language-modeling attribution. All base LMs and trained memory experts are frozen during evaluation. For the QA benchmarks, ExpM holds question–answer pairs from the training split, and its retrieval weight β\beta, gate, and threshold η\eta are selected on dev folds held out from that split. Training the full stack takes about 1,800 GPU-hours on 8×\timesH200 GPUs, a one-time cost broken down by stage in Appendix A.6.

4.2 Main QA Results

Table 1 reports the factual QA results. MoM attains the highest average on both backbones, improving the frozen backbone by 15.6% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 10.9% on Llama-3.1-8B, and leads MLP Memory, the strongest parametric baseline, by 1.08 points on Mistral. On Mistral, RAG is stronger on TruthfulQA and HotpotQA and the RAG-RL reproduction on NQ and WebQ, but MoM never falls below its frozen backbone on any benchmark, whereas every other method except MLP Memory lowers at least one benchmark. The pattern tracks where each method intervenes. CPT and LoRA rewrite the weights behind every prediction, and their WebQ gains on both backbones come with NQ losses of up to 8.47 points. RAG conditions every answer on retrieved passages and lowers the Llama average by 8.8%. MoM instead leaves the backbone and its input unchanged and acts only on the output distribution. MoM additionally weights each memory per token from uncertainty and disagreement features and lets ExpM answer only when the gate accepts the retrieved fact, so unhelpful memory is down-weighted or skipped.

4.3 Component Analysis

Language modeling channel attribution.

Figure 3 isolates the neural memories on WikiText-103 with GPT2-large and ExpM disabled. LatM with a fixed mixing weight lowers perplexity from 10.45 to 9.58. A token-wise router over Base LM and LatM reaches 9.61, recovering most of this gain without a globally tuned coefficient. Adding LexM lowers perplexity further to 9.37, so the token-space memory contributes information that LatM does not provide. The result shows that the routed core assigns more probability to the observed next token, and with the backbone frozen, this gain reflects knowledge that the neural memories add without changing the backbone weights. Appendix B.2 reports how the router distributes weight across token types on each backbone.

Routed versus external explicit memory.

Figure 5 tests the central design choice of MoM by exposing the same populated store in two ways. As an external overlay, ExpM raises QA score by 7.87–8.86 points on the three benchmarks. As a fourth routed source, the same store adds only 0.75–1.23 points, because the router, trained while the store was empty or sparse, assigns ExpM little mass. The store contents are identical, so the gap reflects allocation rather than memory quality.

Router training with routed ExpM.

Figure 5 shows that the router’s own training objective limits a routed ExpM. Every variant improves over Pure LM, removing either regularizer helps further, and removing the ExpM usage penalty helps most. Both terms oppose the allocation ExpM needs. A stored answer changes a greedy prediction only when its weight lets the stored token win, as the overlay ensures with λt=0.8\lambda_{t}=0.8. The entropy regularizer, which keeps the router from collapsing onto one source, penalizes such peaked allocations, and the usage penalty lowers ExpM mass directly. Learned while the store is empty or sparse, the resulting low ExpM weight persists once the store is populated. Using a stored fact is an all-or-nothing decision per question, which suits an answer-level gate better than a token-level softmax trained before the fact is written.

4.4 Explicit Memory Updates

We test whether written facts take effect immediately and whether writing them disturbs answers the model already gets right. For each backbone, we draw two disjoint sets of 200 questions from the NQ-open training split, excluding the dev folds and all questions used to train or calibrate ExpM: DnewD_{\text{new}}, which both the base LM and the routed core answer incorrectly, and DoldD_{\text{old}}, which both answer correctly. We write the DnewD_{\text{new}} facts, one answer each, into an empty store and evaluate both sets with the QA configuration of Table 1. Since DnewD_{\text{new}} is queried with the questions used for writing, its score measures how reliably a written fact is read back, not generalization to rephrased questions.

Figure 7 shows that the writes take effect immediately and leave DoldD_{\text{old}} almost untouched. EM on DnewD_{\text{new}} rises from 0.50 on both backbones to 100.00 on Llama and 99.50 on Mistral. Since no DoldD_{\text{old}} fact is written, a DoldD_{\text{old}} answer can change only if the gate accepts an entry retrieved for an unrelated question. This happens once in 400 queries: on Llama, the release year of Call Me by Your Name changes from the correct 2017 to “May 11, 2018,” lowering EM from 99.00 to 98.50.

4.5 Efficiency

Figure 7 compares time to first token (TTFT) and decoding throughput (TPS). RAG and kkNN-LM raise TTFT from 32 ms to 135 and 130 ms and lower throughput from 53 to 25 and 9 tokens/s. Both put a search over an external index on the critical path, RAG also prefills the retrieved passages, and kkNN-LM searches its datastore at every decoding step. MoM with the full router reaches 45 ms and 35 tokens/s, a 2.9–3.0×\times lower TTFT than the two retrieval methods. Compared with the frozen base model, this is a 1.4×\times higher TTFT and 66% of its decoding throughput. Appendix A.6 reports memory, storage, and training costs.

5 Conclusion

We presented Mixture-of-Memories (MoM), a memory-augmented language modeling framework that routes stable neural memories token by token and handles factual updates through a writable explicit memory outside the router. MoM lowers WikiText-103 perplexity and obtains the best average factual QA score on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and Llama-3.1-8B, with a lower time to first token than retrieval-augmented baselines. The same populated store helps far more as an external overlay than as a routed source, and written facts take effect immediately while previously correct answers are almost all preserved. Future work can extend MoM to other knowledge-intensive NLP tasks and to settings where knowledge changes continuously.

Limitations

The proposed method has two main limitations. First, the explicit memory selects a single fact for each question from the whole store: as the store grows, more entries compete for each query, which raises the chance that a wrong fact is retrieved and accepted, making the current design more suitable for targeted factual updates than very large memory stores. Second, although our results are strong on QA benchmarks, the present evaluation is still concentrated on knowledge-intensive question answering. Further validation on a broader set of NLP tasks is needed to assess the generality of the approach.

Appendix A Experimental Details

A.1 Datasets and Splits

WikiText-103 is used for GPT2-large language modeling. Wikipedia-2021 is used for memory training, CPT, the kkNN-LM datastore, and the RAG corpus. The QA evaluation uses the full evaluation splits of Natural Questions (3,610 questions), HotpotQA (7,405), WebQuestions (2,032), TriviaQA (17,944), and TruthfulQA. For the update experiments, DnewD_{\mathrm{new}} and DoldD_{\mathrm{old}} each contain 200 questions from the NQ-open training split, selected separately for each backbone (Section 4.4). The facts of DnewD_{\mathrm{new}} are written into an initially empty store, and DoldD_{\mathrm{old}} is never written. We report score after all 200 writes.

A.2 Baselines

Parametric baselines.

CPT updates all parameters of the backbone by continued pretraining with the language-modeling objective. LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) keeps the backbone frozen and learns low-rank updates to its weight matrices. MLP Memory (Wei et al., 2025) is a pretrained MLP that imitates the next-token distribution of a nearest-neighbor retriever, and its output is interpolated with the distribution of the frozen backbone.

Retrieval baselines.

RAG retrieves the top-5 Wikipedia passages for each question with a BGE retriever (Xiao et al., 2024) and prepends them to the backbone’s prompt. kkNN-LM (Khandelwal et al., 2020) interpolates the backbone’s next-token distribution with the next tokens of the nearest stored contexts, retrieved from a 50M-key datastore stored with product quantization.

Post-trained RAG reproduction.

RAG-RL (Huang et al., 2025) trains the reader with reinforcement learning and curriculum learning. We implemented a paper-guided reproduction with a bge-base-en-v1.5 retriever, exact inner-product FAISS search over 200,000 uniformly sampled Wikipedia-2021 chunks, question-only queries, top-5 retrieval, greedy bf16 decoding, and seed 42, with Mistral-7B-v0.3 as the reader backbone.

A.3 Metrics

For open-domain QA, EM is computed after answer normalization and measures whether the generated answer exactly matches any accepted answer alias. F1 is the token-level overlap after the same normalization. We report F1 for NQ. For TruthfulQA, we use the official multiple-choice suite: MC1 measures whether the single best answer is preferred, MC2 measures the total probability assigned to true answers relative to false answers, and MC3 measures the fraction of true answers ranked above false answers. We report their average when a single TruthfulQA score is needed.

A.4 ExpM Configuration

The Budget Router outputs weights over Base, LatM, and LexM only, and the routed core is trained separately from ExpM. The ExpM encoders read the frozen backbone feature of Eq. 11 with a 32-token averaging window. For the QA benchmarks, ExpM retrieves the top-scoring entry over the whole store with the score of Eq. 12, computes the agreement feature from the top-kk entries, and injects the retrieved answer with λ=0.8\lambda=0.8 when the gate accepts it. On the dev folds, β\beta is chosen from {0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1}\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1\} and kk from {4,8,16}\{4,8,16\}, so the β\beta used at test time can differ across benchmarks and backbones. TriviaQA answers have many valid surface forms, so each TriviaQA training question is written with up to ten answer aliases; evaluation still uses the official normalized scorer, which accepts any annotated alias. The encoders are not retrained for the QA experiments. Only the answer-level gate is fitted.

A.5 Hyperparameter Selection

In the QA experiments, the gate threshold is η=0.35\eta=0.35 for NQ, WebQ, and HotpotQA on both backbones, and 0.50.5 (Mistral) and 0.80.8 (Llama) for TriviaQA. Ablations use λ=0.4\lambda=0.4 unless they sweep the value. We report full test-set results for the main tables.

A.6 Training Cost and Deployment Overhead

Training takes about 1,800 H200 GPU-hours once: about 400 for the kkNN teacher targets, 1,100 for LatM distillation, 150 for LexM, 50 for the router, and 100 for preprocessing and pipeline overhead. The stages run sequentially with the base LM frozen, and afterwards new facts enter only through ExpM writes.

With a 7B backbone, LatM (1.0B parameters, 2.0 GB in bf16), LexM (0.77B, 1.55 GB), and the 580-parameter router raise resident weights from 14.0 GB to 17.6 GB. The ExpM store has no trainable parameters, occupies about 15 MB, and grows with the number of written facts, whereas our product-quantized kkNN-LM datastore occupies 3.2 GB. Both neural memories are MLPs that add about 6⋅nlayer⋅dmodel⋅dff6\cdot n_{\text{layer}}\cdot d_{\text{model}}\cdot d_{\text{ff}} FLOPs per token, and ExpM retrieves once per question rather than per token.

Appendix B Supplementary Experiments

B.1 Cross-Backbone Transfer of Lexical Memory

LexM consumes token IDs, so it can be moved to another backbone. We transplant a Mistral-trained LexM into Llama-3.1-8B through a token-string mapping between the two vocabularies, which changes 8.27% of the target embedding rows and requires no retraining. Table 2 shows that the transplanted LexM keeps EM within 0.20 points of the Llama backbone on all three benchmarks, so it can be attached without disrupting the base model but adds no knowledge in this setting. In contrast, a LexM trained on Llama itself raises NQ EM from 17.15 to 19.47 with a fixed weight of 0.25, while changing TriviaQA EM by at most 0.35 points.

B.2 Router Gate Interpretability

To test whether the router learns non-trivial token-wise allocation, we group generated tokens into semantic, numeric, and syntactic categories, represented by ENTITY, NUMBER, and PUNCT tokens, and compute the average gate weight of each memory channel. The allocation depends on both the token type and the backbone. On Mistral, punctuation tokens are routed mostly to the base LM (gate weight 0.908 on PUNCT), while NUMBER tokens receive a larger LatM weight of 0.286, so LatM is used selectively on factual or numeric positions. On Llama, LexM dominates, with gate weights of 0.614, 0.698, and 0.749 on ENTITY, NUMBER, and PUNCT, while LatM receives only 0.7–1.2% of the mass. The router therefore adapts its memory usage to token semantics and to the quality of each channel on a given backbone rather than following a static interpolation rule.

B.3 Case Study

Figure 8 shows a case study. For the question of who was originally cast as Indiana Jones, RAG retrieves passages that contain both “Indiana Jones” and the phrase “originally was cast.” The retrieved evidence, however, states that Paul Picerni was originally cast in a different role. RAG copies this entity and answers “Paul Picerni,” the base LM answers “Steve McQueen,” and CPT, LoRA, and MLP Memory also return plausible but incorrect actors. MoM returns the gold answer, “Tom Selleck,” showing that ExpM can recover a written fact even when lexical retrieval is misled by entity and phrase overlap.
